newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan plans 2-3 year domestic bond next year.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan plans 2-3 year domestic bond next year.

text.p: Kazakhstan plans to extend maturities in its government securities market next year with a two- or three-year bond, a top central bank official said on Wednesday.
National Bank of Kazakhstan deputy chairman Grigory Marchenko said the bank also hoped to launch full-scale open market operations in 1997.

The finance ministry currently auctions three-month GKO discount Treasury bills every Tuesday, six-month bills twice a month on Mondays, and since July 12-month bills about once a month on Mondays, he told Reuters in an interview.
Auctions of 12-month paper could be stepped up to twice a month, and next year will see a two or three-year bond, he said.
"The issue is -- should it be a coupon. If it's a coupon it should probably be floating rate," Marchenko said.
Last month the finance ministry issued its first savings bond, on which interest is tied to GKO yields.
The average yield on the latest issue of six-month paper, auctioned on Tuesday, was 37.33 percent. Annual inflation this year is likely to be 29 percent, Marchenko said.
Proposals to issue a dollar-denominated domestic bond have been rejected by the finance ministry, which feared the paper would hamper dedollarisation of the economy.
A debut $100 million three-year Eurobond is likely to be launched by the end of the year, however.
The central bank plans to use both repos and outright sales in the T-bill market to manage liquidity.
"We believe we will be able to use open-market operations as a primary tool by the end of 1997," Marchenko said.
The small size of the Treasury bill market and of the central bank's portfolio has hampered the start of open-market operations so far, he said.
Outstanding T-bills total 12 billion tenge ($170 million) at discount, compared with total money supply of nearly $2 billion.
The central bank's portfolio of T-bills ranks only third among those of the 17 primary dealers. "Our share of the market is less than 15 percent," Marchenko said.
But it has been testing repos since April this year.
"We're conducting repos to get primary dealers up the learning curve," he said.
Banks increasingly prefer to conduct T-bill repos with each other rather than lending outright in the interbank credit market, following last summer's Russian banking crisis, he said.
The size of the market has also kept foreign investors away.
"One of the reasons they're not investing actively is the small size of the market," Marchenko said.
Investors willing to invest in Kazakhstan are effectively limited to the T-bill market, because equity market infrastructure such as depositories is still inadequate.
But a potential investor's country limit for Kazakhstan can be many times the volume of a single T-bill issue, typically around 500 million tenge ($7 million).
The finance ministry sets limits for foreign investment on each issue, usually 20 percent, but there are no limits on foreign acquisitions in the secondary market, Marchenko said.
